claims.text: Integrating first-principles phonon-dispersion calculations with machine learning informed by HEA configurational metrics will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than average-composition or lattice-parameter methods.
HfNbTaTiZr is an equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy that can be prepared through powder-based additive manufacturing.
Processed equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can exhibit a near-single-phase beta-BCC structure or a controlled multiphase structure.
Controlled synthesis can minimize inhomogeneous phase formation and defect concentration in screened HEAs.
Temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C are relevant operating conditions for HEA thermal-insulation applications.
Controlling the atmosphere can limit extraneous oxidation or phase transformations during high-temperature testing.
Microstructural uniformity and defect levels, including interstitial oxygen content, influence phonon scattering and thermal conductivity in HEAs.
Detailed phonon-dispersion information captures scattering caused by atomic-scale disorder and interstitials.
Combining phonon-dispersion information with configurational-entropy metrics will make computed vibrational densities of states correlate more directly with low phonon thermal conductivity.
The integrated approach will outperform traditional compositional metrics.
The approach will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by at least 20–30% over current methods.
The approach will consistently identify HEAs exhibiting reduced phonon-mediated thermal conduction.
Current prediction models primarily use averaged composition, mass, or lattice-parameter correlations and omit detailed vibrational and microstructural variation.
The claimed accuracy improvement is limited to HEAs with limited phase inhomogeneity and controlled defect concentrations.
Significant uncontrolled multiphase formation or high defect density will degrade the predictive approach's accuracy.
Datasets directly linking HEA phonon conductivity to configurational entropy are limited.
A benchmark spanning room temperature to approximately 1000 °C can compare integrated-model predictions with traditional-model predictions and measured thermal conductivity.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant 20–30% prediction improvement, or failure to establish the proposed vibrational-profile correlation, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome concerns a 20–30% improvement in prediction accuracy, whereas the falsification rule asks whether measured thermal conductivities show a 20–30% reduction relative to traditional predictions. Reduction in conductivity is not the same quantity as improvement in predictive accuracy; an error metric such as MAE or RMSE is not defined.

The hypothesis invokes disorder- and defect-induced phonon scattering as a route to low conductivity, but the falsification rule refers to 'predicted low phonon scattering.' This reverses or at least obscures the proposed scattering relationship.
